name: Mengerei

catalog_citation: Harris, Joy Kinslow. 1969. Descriptive and comparative study of the Gunwingguan languages, Northern Territory. PhD thesis, Australian National University. 189 pp. ANU Open Research handle 1885/132713 (open).
catalog_locator: Part III, sec. 2.2 'The Verbal Imperative Clause', p. 84; nine-language citation paradigm with the Mengerei row p. 83. Supporting: Appendix I 'Sketch of Gunbalang phonemics', STRESS AND INTONATION p. 172 and NOTES ON OTHER LANGUAGES p. 173.
catalog_quote: The imperative clauses are distinct from the declarative in several features: (1) the absence of a subject tagmeme; (2) the occurrence of the person prefix on the verb limited to second person singular as subject, though it occurs in combination with any other person as object; (3) an imperative stress pattern with primary stress on the person prefix rather than, as elsewhere, on the verb root. Other than Gunaviji, all of the above evidence these distinctions. [p. 84; the p. 83 citation paradigm 'The Verbal Imperative Clause' lists nine languages incl. Mengerei: ag-pirr 'you go back', ag-aniynak 'you it light', a-rrum 'you say'] ... Primary stress occurs on the initial syllable of each root except when compounds are formed of more than one root, then primary stress occurs on the penultimate syllable. [Appendix I, Sketch of Gunbalang phonemics, STRESS AND INTONATION, p. 172] ... Mengerei and Maung have the same phonemes as Gunbalang, but have vowel initial syllables, e.g. Mengerei: /ulanjŋam/ 'cave', Maung: /ararkpi/ 'man'. [NOTES ON OTHER LANGUAGES, p. 173]

new_statements.rule_in_words: For Mengerei (Mangerr), as for the other eight languages Harris compares (all but Gunaviji), primary stress in the verb falls on the verb root rather than on the person prefix; in imperatives it shifts to the person prefix. Harris's explicit syllable-level rule (primary stress on the initial syllable of each root; penultimate in root compounds) is stated only for Gunbalang; for Mengerei she says only that its phonemes match Gunbalang's but that it allows vowel-initial syllables, so the initial-syllable-of-root detail is not explicitly asserted for Mangerr.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for any of the languages.
new_statements.exceptions: Imperative verbs: primary stress on the second-person prefix instead of the root. (Gunbalang only: root compounds take penultimate primary stress.)
new_statements.domain_note: Verb word only, from elicited citation-paradigm sentences ('go away!', 'burn it!', 'tell me!'); no statement on nominal stress for Mengerei. Data from a single speaker at Oenpelli in the 1960s, when the language was already nearly extinct. The statement is a comparative generalisation over nine languages, not a Mengerei-specific phonology.
new_statements.identity_note: Harris 1969 calls the language 'Mengerei'; Glottolog's language code mapping for that thesis equates Mengerei with Mangerr [zme] (mang1382; AIATSIS N53 Mengerrdji). Her data come from one remaining first-language speaker at Oenpelli (Gunbalanya) in the 1960s. The Campbell 2006 sketch and Birch 2006 dictionary treat Mengerrdji together with Erre (erre1238) and Urningangk (urni1239) as the three Giimbiyu varieties.

sources.note: Mengerei (= Mangerr) is one of nine languages compared. p.84: imperative clauses in all nine languages except Gunaviji show 'an imperative stress pattern with primary stress on the person prefix rather than, as elsewhere, on the verb root' (paradigm p.83 includes Mengerei). Appendix I p.172 gives the explicit Gunbalang rule (primary stress on the initial syllable of each root; penultimate in compounds); p.173 says only that 'Mengerei and Maung have the same phonemes as Gunbalang, but have vowel initial syllables' — the stress rule is not explicitly extended to Mengerei.
